opus-5.5.text:
So the ensemble results are really informative, and I think they tell you something important about the strengths and the limitations of the original ARC-AGI dataset.

Back in 2020, after the first Kaggle competition, we took all the submissions and ensembled them. Individually, the top entries were around 20% on the private set, but if you pooled everything together you got to roughly 49%. That told us that about half the private evaluation tasks were, in principle, solvable by some combination of brute-force program search over hand-crafted DSLs. None of those systems were intelligent in any meaningful sense. They were enumerating programs. So already in 2020 you could see that a decent chunk of ARC-AGI-1 was vulnerable to brute force, given enough compute and a good enough DSL.

Then in 2024 we did a similar exercise, and an ensemble of the competition entries got somewhere around 80%. That's a big number, and it's a big number partly because the 2024 approaches were genuinely new and interesting, with test-time training, program synthesis guided by LLMs, and so on. Those are real conceptual advances toward test-time adaptation. But it also confirms that the dataset had a ceiling on how much signal it could give you. A lot of the tasks were too similar to each other, too similar to things in the public set, or simple enough that you could get them with search rather than with genuine on-the-fly abstraction.

So what it reveals is twofold. First, ARC did its job. It wasn't saturated by scaling up pretraining. Plain LLMs stayed near zero for years. What finally moved the needle was a shift toward test-time adaptation, which is exactly the thing the benchmark was designed to reward. Second, it's not a perfect measure. A single score on ARC-AGI-1 conflates real fluid intelligence with brute-force coverage. That's precisely why we built ARC-AGI-2: to remove tasks that are susceptible to brute force, to make tasks require more compositional reasoning, and to calibrate everything against human testers so we know each task is solvable by people.

The broader lesson is that no benchmark is a final, static measure of AGI. A benchmark is a tool that points you in the right direction at a given moment. Once it stops being informative, you need to evolve it. The way I'd put it is: you'll know we have AGI when it becomes impossible to create tasks that are easy for humans and hard for AI. We're not there yet.

r001.rationale: It says the 2020 ensemble reached roughly 49% and that about half the private tasks were solvable through brute-force program search.

r002.rationale: It calls ARC-AGI-1 an imperfect measure because its score conflates fluid intelligence with brute-force coverage, citing the high ensemble score and search-solvable tasks.

r003.rationale: It reports the 2024 ensemble score of around 80%, but does not discuss a passing threshold or state that reaching it would not imply proximity to AGI.

r004.rationale: It says brute-force search could solve about half the private tasks, but does not argue that scaling computation will eventually solve the full ARC challenge.

r005.rationale: It identifies the dataset’s ceiling and tasks susceptible to brute force as reasons for building ARC-AGI-2.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the ensemble results are actually one of the more revealing things to come out of those competitions, and they point in a slightly uncomfortable direction for anyone who wants to read ARC scores as a straight line toward AGI.

Let me explain what I mean. In 2020, the top solutions were almost entirely hand-crafted program search, DSLs written by humans, with brute-force enumeration over those primitives. Individually, the winning approaches were scoring around 20 percent on the private test set. But when you ensembled them, when you took the top handful of entries and combined their outputs, you got a meaningful jump, something closer to 49 percent. And that's a tell. If the solutions were capturing some general, shared capability, you wouldn't expect them to be that complementary. The fact that stacking them helps so much means each one is solving a different, fairly narrow slice of the task distribution. They're overfit to particular kinds of transformations. Each DSL encodes its author's intuitions about which concepts matter, and those intuitions don't overlap much.

Then in 2024 you see a similar pattern, but with a different substrate. The dominant techniques became test-time training on transductive models, and LLM-guided program synthesis on the inductive side. The best individual entries got into the mid-50s. And again, if you ensemble the transductive approaches with the inductive, program-search approaches, you get a jump, because they fail on very different tasks. The transductive models are good at perceptual, local pattern completion. The program synthesis approaches are good at tasks with clean, compositional structure. They're almost orthogonal in where they succeed.

So what does that reveal about the benchmark? A few things.

First, it confirms that ARC is doing what it was designed to do, which is to resist being solved by any single narrow trick. If one approach solved it, that would mean the benchmark had a shortcut. The fact that you need to glue together very different approaches, and that even then you're not at human level, suggests the task diversity is real.

Second, and this is the important caveat, it means you have to be careful about what a top-line number is actually measuring. A score of 55 percent from an ensemble of specialized methods is not the same thing as 55 percent from a single system with a general ability to acquire new skills. The number doesn't distinguish between those. And the whole point of ARC was to measure skill acquisition efficiency, the ability to adapt to genuinely novel problems with very little data. An ensemble that works because somebody pre-selected which approach handles which task shape is, in a sense, smuggling in human intelligence through the back door. It's the researchers doing the generalization, not the system.

Third, the gap between ensemble performance and single-model performance is a nice diagnostic. If that gap closes, if a single system starts matching or exceeding what you can get by ensembling many specialized ones, that's a much stronger signal of general capability than the raw score going up. In 2024 that gap was still wide. That tells me we're still in the regime of accumulating partial solutions rather than discovering a fundamentally general mechanism.

And honestly, this is part of why we built ARC-AGI-2 the way we did. ARC-1 was saturating in a way that didn't feel like it was tracking the thing we cared about. It was tracking the ability of the community to throw compute and clever engineering at the problem, which is fine, that's real progress of a kind, but it's not the same as closing the gap on fluid intelligence. So the lesson from the ensembles is: the benchmark is measuring something real, but the headline number alone can't tell you whether you're looking at generality or a patchwork. You have to look at the structure of the solutions, how much compute they burn per task, how much human prior knowledge is baked in, and how well a single system transfers across the whole distribution. Those are the things that actually tell you about progress toward AGI.

astra-6.text:
I think the ensemble results highlight a distinction between doing well on a benchmark and developing a general capability. If you combine systems with different strengths, you can solve more tasks because their failures don’t completely overlap. That’s useful, but the higher score doesn’t, by itself, tell you that you’ve built a more general learner.

For ARC, the question is how a system acquires a solution to something new. Is it discovering the relevant abstraction from the few examples it’s given, or are we expanding a collection of approaches until one happens to cover the task? Both can improve benchmark performance, but they imply different things about progress toward AGI.

So I would interpret ensemble gains cautiously. You need to look at the individual systems, how much prior knowledge and computation they use, and whether the improvement carries over to genuinely unfamiliar tasks. ARC is a way to probe generalization; its score isn’t a direct measurement of how close we are to AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they highlight a distinction between doing well on a benchmark and acquiring a general capability. In both competitions, combining systems with different strengths could improve the score because they solved different subsets of the tasks. But the ensemble score doesn’t, by itself, tell you that any of those systems has become more general.

Imagine accumulating specialized approaches, each covering another little pocket of the benchmark. You can make progress that way without solving the underlying problem of efficiently acquiring new skills. And that’s what ARC is intended to probe: how well you can adapt to a novel task from very little information.

That doesn’t make ensembles illegitimate, or the benchmark useless. It means you have to interpret the score alongside the resources and prior knowledge used to obtain it. How much engineering went into the system? How much task-specific knowledge? How much computation does it spend at test time?

So I would take those results as evidence of progress on ARC, but not automatically as equivalent progress toward AGI. The stronger evidence would be a system that continues to adapt efficiently to genuinely new tasks, beyond the particular distribution we’ve learned to optimize for.
